topic: Inspection concepts, measuring tools and NDT

notes.front: In the handbook’s sense, what is an inspection?
notes.back: A visual examination and manual checks to determine the condition of an aircraft or component.
notes.explanation: It can range from a casual walk around to a detailed inspection with complete disassembly and complex inspection aids.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Inspection Concepts & Techniques”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Inspections are visual examinations and manual checks to determine the condition of an aircraft or component.
notes.example: Like a doctor’s check-up for an aircraft: sometimes a glance and a few questions, sometimes a full set of scans.

notes.front: What are preflight and postflight inspections?
notes.back: Before flight, the pilot follows the preflight checklist, including a walk-around; after flight, a postflight inspection looks for problems needing repair or servicing.
notes.explanation: The handbook recommends the postflight check be done by the pilot or a mechanic, so faults are caught before the next flight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Preflight/Postflight Inspections”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: After each flight, it is recommended that the pilot or mechanic conduct a postflight inspection to detect any problems that might require repair or servicing before the next flight.
notes.example: Like checking your car’s tyres and oil before a trip, then noting any new rattle when you park.

notes.front: What is nondestructive testing (NDT)?
notes.back: Methods that determine the airworthiness of a component without damaging it; the handbook also calls it nondestructive inspection.
notes.explanation: Some NDT methods are simple and need little extra expertise; others are highly sophisticated and need specially certified technicians.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Nondestructive Inspection/Testing”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: The objective of NDI and NDT is to determine the airworthiness of a component, without damaging it, that would render it unairworthy.
notes.example: Like an X-ray of a broken arm: you learn what is inside without cutting anything open.

notes.front: What is a borescope?
notes.back: A device that lets the inspector see inside areas that could not otherwise be inspected without disassembly.
notes.explanation: Inspection with a borescope is essentially a visual inspection, used to reduce or eliminate costly teardowns.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Borescope”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: A borescope is a device that enables the inspector to see inside areas that could not otherwise be inspected without disassembly.
notes.example: Like a keyhole camera, but threaded into an engine’s access port instead of a door.

notes.front: What is penetrant inspection?
notes.back: A nondestructive test for defects open to the surface in parts made of any nonporous material.
notes.explanation: A penetrating liquid enters a surface opening and stays there, making the defect clearly visible.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Liquid Penetrant Inspection”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: Penetrant inspection is a nondestructive test for defects open to the surface in parts made of any nonporous material.
notes.example: Like wiping ink across a cracked tile and then cleaning the surface: the ink left in the crack shows where it runs.

notes.front: What is ultrasonic inspection?
notes.back: A nondestructive technique that sends sound energy through the test specimen to detect flaws.
notes.explanation: The sound passing through the specimen is shown on a display, where front and back surfaces and internal conditions appear as signals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Ultrasonic Inspection”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: Ultrasonic inspection is an NDI technique that uses sound energy moving through the test specimen to detect flaws.
notes.example: Like a ship’s echo sounder finding the seabed, but finding cracks inside a metal part.

notes.front: What is a couplant in ultrasonic inspection?
notes.back: A layer of material that couples the transducer to the test piece.
notes.explanation: It is required because ultrasonic energy does not travel through air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Couplants”, p. 10-26
notes.evidence: A layer of couplant is required to couple the transducer to the test piece, because ultrasonic energy does not travel through air.
notes.example: Like the gel a medical scanner uses on skin; typical ultrasonic couplants are water, glycerin, motor oils and grease.

notes.front: How is acoustic emission inspection carried out?
notes.back: Acoustic emission sensors are placed at various points on the structure, which is then put under a load or stress.
notes.explanation: Flaws such as cracks emit sound waves under stress, and the sensors register those bursts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Acoustic Emission Inspection”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: on an aircraft structure and then applying a load or stress.
notes.example: Like listening for creaks in a wooden floor as someone walks across it.

notes.front: What is magnetic particle inspection?
notes.back: A method of detecting invisible cracks and other defects in ferromagnetic materials, such as iron and steel.
notes.explanation: The part is magnetised and ferromagnetic particles are applied; the handbook says it is not applicable to nonmagnetic materials.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnetic Particle Inspection”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: Magnetic particle inspection is a method of detecting invisible cracks and other defects in ferromagnetic materials, such as iron and steel. It is not applicable to nonmagnetic materials.
notes.example: Like sprinkling iron filings over a magnet, where the filings bunch up at the gap in a cracked part.

notes.front: What is Magnaglo inspection?
notes.back: A magnetic particle method that uses a fluorescent particle solution and is inspected under black light.
notes.explanation: The neon-like glow of defects lets smaller flaw indications be seen, which increases the efficiency of inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnaglo Inspection”, p. 10-32
notes.evidence: Magnaglo inspection is similar to the preceding method, but differs in that a fluorescent particle solution is used and the inspection is made under black light.
notes.example: Like ordinary magnetic particle inspection, but the indications glow under a black light.

notes.front: What is demagnetising, after magnetic particle inspection?
notes.back: Removing the permanent magnetism left in the part after inspection, required if the part is to return to service.
notes.explanation: The handbook requires it for parts going back into service; magnetism left in them can attract particles or affect instruments.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Demagnetizing”, p. 10-33
notes.evidence: The permanent magnetism remaining after inspection must be removed by a demagnetization operation if the part is to be returned to service.
notes.example: Like wiping a fridge magnet’s effect off a screwdriver so it stops picking up screws.

notes.front: What is radiography in aircraft inspection?
notes.back: X or gamma radiation is projected through a part onto film, which after processing becomes a radiograph, or shadow picture, of the object.
notes.explanation: The radiation’s ability to penetrate material and disclose discontinuities is what makes it useful for inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Radiographic”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: The penetrating radiation is projected through the part to be inspected and produces an invisible or latent image in the film. When processed, the film becomes a radiograph or shadow picture of the object.
notes.example: Like a hospital X-ray of a bone, but of a wing structure or an engine.

notes.front: What is a tap test?
notes.back: A quick check of an accessible surface for delamination or debonding by lightly tapping it and listening to the response.
notes.explanation: The handbook also calls it the ring test or coin test, and it is widely used on composite structures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Tap Testing”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: Tap testing, also referred to as the ring test or coin test, is widely used as a quick evaluation of any accessible surface
notes.example: Like tapping a wall to find a stud: the sound changes where the structure behind is different.

notes.front: What is thermography?
notes.back: A nondestructive technique, often used on thin composite structures, that uses radiant electromagnetic thermal energy to detect flaws.
notes.explanation: It measures or maps surface temperatures as heat flows from, to or through the test object.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Thermography”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: Thermography is an NDI technique often used with thin composite structures that use radiant electromagnetic thermal energy to detect flaws.
notes.example: Like a thermal camera spotting where a house loses heat, but finding disbonds in a panel.

notes.front: In composite repair, what does an electrical conductivity test check?
notes.back: That the conductive path built into the structure has been restored, checked with an ohmmeter.
notes.explanation: Composites are not inherently conductive, so some aircraft have aluminium or copper embedded in the plies, and a repair must keep that path continuous.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrical Conductivity”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: Electrical conductivity may be checked by use of an ohmmeter. Specific manufacturer’s instructions must be carefully followed.
notes.example: Like checking a mended extension lead with a continuity tester before plugging it in.

notes.front: What do a tap and a die do?
notes.back: A tap cuts threads on the inside of a hole; a die cuts external threads on round stock.
notes.explanation: Both are made of hard tempered steel and ground to an exact size.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Taps and Dies”, p. 11-14
notes.evidence: A tap is used to cut threads on the inside of a hole, while a die is for cutting external threads on round stock.
notes.example: Like a nut and a bolt: the tap makes the inside thread a bolt screws into; the die makes the bolt’s own thread.

notes.front: What are rules, as layout and measuring tools?
notes.back: Steel rules, rigid or flexible, marked in common fractions or in decimals, used as a measuring tool or a straightedge.
notes.explanation: In aircraft work the inch is the unit most commonly used, divided into common or decimal fractions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Rules”, p. 11-14
notes.evidence: Rules are made of steel and are either rigid or flexible.
notes.example: Like a school ruler, but made of steel and marked down to sixty-fourths or hundredths of an inch.

notes.front: What is a combination set?
notes.back: A blade (rule) with a sliding head that can be clamped anywhere; the square or stock head carries a level and scriber.
notes.explanation: It does the job of a tri-square, but its head slides along the blade and can be clamped at any place.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Combination Sets”, p. 11-17
notes.evidence: It can be used for the same purposes as an ordinary tri-square, but it differs from the tri-square in that the head slides along the blade and can be clamped at any desired place.
notes.example: Like a carpenter’s square with a built-in spirit level and a movable head.

notes.front: What are dividers?
notes.back: Two legs joined at the top by a pivot, both tapered to needle points, used to scribe circles and arcs and transfer measurements.
notes.explanation: Pencil compasses look the same but carry a pencil on one leg.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Dividers and Pencil Compasses”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: Dividers and pencil compasses have two legs joined at the top by a pivot. They are used to scribe circles and arcs and for transferring measurements from the rule to the work.
notes.example: Like a school compass, but with two steel points instead of a pencil.

notes.front: What is a micrometer used for?
notes.back: Measuring more closely than a steel rule can, in thousandths and ten-thousandths of an inch.
notes.explanation: The steel rule reads only to one sixty-fourth in fractions or one hundredth in decimals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Micrometer Calipers”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: To measure more closely than this (in thousandths and ten-thousandths of an inch), a micrometer is used.
notes.example: Like a ruler with a fine screw thread that lets you read the thickness of a sheet of metal.

notes.front: On a micrometer, what does a vernier scale add?
notes.back: It lets you read directly the fraction of a thimble division, to ten-thousandths of an inch.
notes.explanation: Its graduations divide 0.001 inch into 10 equal parts of 0.0001 inch each.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Vernier Scale”, p. 11-23
notes.evidence: Some micrometers are equipped with a vernier scale that makes it possible to directly read the fraction of a division that is indicated on the thimble scale.
notes.example: Like adding a finer second hand to a clock that otherwise shows only minutes.

notes.front: Which ACS element names the vernier caliper, and how?
notes.back: A skill element: the applicant demonstrates the ability to use Vernier calipers.
notes.explanation: It sits beside using micrometers and measurement gauges among the inspection skills of the General knowledge area.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, K. Inspection Concepts and Techniques”, p. 17
notes.evidence: AM.I.K.S1 Use Vernier calipers. AM.I.K.S2 Use micrometers. AM.I.K.S3 Use measurement gauges.
notes.example: Like the slide caliper the handbook describes: jaws slid along a graduated scale to measure inside or outside sizes.

notes.front: What is a dial indicator?
notes.back: A variation of the micrometer that measures variations in a surface with a machined probe linked to a circular hand.
notes.explanation: The hand’s movement shows thousandths of an inch, or the reading appears on a liquid crystal screen.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Using a Micrometer”, p. 11-24
notes.evidence: A variation of the micrometer is the dial indicator, which measures variations in a surface by using an accurately machined probe mechanically-linked to a circular hand whose movement indicates thousandths of an inch
notes.example: Like a car’s speedometer needle, but moved by a probe resting on a spinning shaft.

notes.front: What does calibrating a torque wrench achieve?
notes.back: It ensures the wrench produces a precise torque on a standard and consistent basis.
notes.explanation: Regular calibration gives repeatable accuracy; the ACS lists calibration and tool accuracy requirements as knowledge to test.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Torque Wrench”, p. 11-6
notes.evidence: Calibrating a torque wrench is the process in which the manufacturers of the torque wrench set ensure a precise torque occurs on a standard and consistent basis.
notes.example: Like checking kitchen scales against a known weight before baking.

notes.front: Where does the ACS place non-invasive condition-monitoring technologies?
notes.back: Among the risk management elements of the Human Factors area.
notes.explanation: The ACS gives no definition; as a risk management element, the applicant must be able to identify, assess and mitigate the risks associated with it.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “I. General, L. Human Factors”, p. 18
notes.evidence: AM.I.L.R2 Fatigue management and fitness for duty. AM.I.L.R3 Non-invasive, condition-monitoring technologies.
notes.example: Like fatigue management, listed just before it, it is a risk the applicant must identify, assess and mitigate.

notes.front: An aircraft inspection can range from {{c1::a casual walk around}} to a detailed inspection involving complete disassembly.
notes.back: A casual walk around.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that detailed inspections may use complex inspection aids.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Inspection Concepts & Techniques”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: An aircraft inspection can range from a casual walk around to a detailed inspection involving complete disassembly and the use of complex inspection aids.

notes.front: What does the handbook call the backbone of a good maintenance programme?
notes.back: Thorough and repeated inspections.
notes.explanation: By contrast, irregular and haphazard inspections invariably result in gradual and certain deterioration of an aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Inspection Concepts & Techniques”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Thorough and repeated inspections must be considered the backbone of a good maintenance program. Irregular and haphazard inspections invariably result in gradual and certain deterioration of an aircraft.

notes.front: What are the two inspection systems aircraft may be inspected under (they may also be combined)?
notes.back: A flight hours inspection system and a calendar inspection system.
notes.explanation: Under the calendar system the inspection falls due after a specified number of calendar weeks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Inspection Concepts & Techniques”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Aircraft may be inspected using a flight hours inspection system, a calendar inspection system, or a combination of both.

notes.front: Before starting an inspection, what must be opened or removed, and what must be done to the structure?
notes.back: All plates, access doors, fairings and cowling opened or removed, and the structure cleaned.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that you note any oil or fluid leakage before cleaning the area.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Basic Inspection Techniques/Practices”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: Before starting an inspection, be certain all plates, access doors, fairings, and cowling have been opened or removed and the structure cleaned.

notes.front: Whose checklist may you use for an inspection?
notes.back: Your own design, one from the equipment’s manufacturer, or one from some other source.
notes.explanation: The rule is simply to always use a checklist so that no items are forgotten or overlooked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Checklists”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: Always use a checklist when performing an inspection. The checklist may be of your own design, one provided by the manufacturer of the equipment being inspected, or one obtained from some other source.

notes.front: According to which specification is the data in a wiring diagram manual organised?
notes.back: The ATA iSpec 2200 specification.
notes.explanation: The manual collects diagrams, drawings and lists defining the wiring and hook-up of installed equipment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Wiring Diagram Manual”, p. 10-4
notes.evidence: The data is organized in accordance with the Air Transport Association ATA iSPec 2200 specification.

notes.front: What is a conformity check during an inspection?
notes.back: Verifying that all installed equipment conforms to the type certificate data sheet, as the aircraft was originally certified.
notes.explanation: Alterations not in the data sheet are covered by a supplemental type certificate, kept with the aircraft’s logs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Type Certificate Data Sheets (TCDS)”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: The inspector ensures that all installed aircraft equipment conforms to the TCDS. This is called a conformity check and verifies that the aircraft conforms to the specifications of the aircraft as it was originally certified.

notes.front: Which aircraft must have the complete inspection every 100 hours, not just annually?
notes.back: Aircraft carrying any person other than a crewmember for hire, or used for flight instruction for hire.
notes.explanation: Such aircraft are likely to be used more frequently than noncommercial aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Annual/100-Hour Inspections”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: Aircraft that are used for commercial purposes (carrying any person, other than a crewmember, for hire or flight instruction for hire) and are likely to be used more frequently than noncommercial aircraft must have this complete inspection every 100 hours.

notes.front: Where is the scope and detail of annual and 100-hour inspections set out?
notes.back: In Appendix D to 14 CFR part 43.
notes.explanation: A properly written checklist includes all the items of Appendix D.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Annual/100-Hour Inspections”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: The scope and detail of items to be included in annual and 100-hour inspections is included as Appendix D to part 43.

notes.front: In a progressive inspection programme, the annual inspection’s scope is divided into phases, typically {{c1::four to six}}.
notes.back: Four to six.
notes.explanation: Completing all phases completes a cycle that satisfies the requirements of an annual inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Progressive Inspections”, p. 10-12
notes.evidence: The scope and detail of an annual inspection is essentially divided into segments or phases (typically four to six).

notes.front: Within what period must a progressive inspection cycle be completed?
notes.back: 12 months.
notes.explanation: If phases remain, they must be done before the end of the 12th month from when the first phase was completed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Progressive Inspections”, p. 10-12
notes.evidence: A cycle must be completed within 12 months. If all required phases are not completed within 12 months, the remaining phase inspections must be conducted before the end of the 12th month from when the first phase was completed.

notes.front: What other name does the handbook give special inspections?
notes.back: Conditional inspections.
notes.explanation: They follow something out of the ordinary that could affect airworthiness, to find whether the structure has been damaged.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Special Inspections”, p. 10-12
notes.evidence: When these situations are encountered, special inspection procedures, also called conditional inspections, are followed to determine if damage to the aircraft structure has occurred.

notes.front: When must an overweight landing inspection be performed?
notes.back: When an aeroplane lands at a weight above the maximum design landing weight.
notes.explanation: The hard landing inspection covers hard landings at or below the maximum design landing limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Hard or Overweight Landing Inspection”, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: An overweight landing inspection must be performed when an airplane lands at a weight above the maximum design landing weight.

notes.front: After a hard landing, what is the most easily detected sign of an excessive load?
notes.back: Wrinkled wing skin.
notes.explanation: Another easily detected indication is fuel leakage along riveted seams.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Hard or Overweight Landing Inspection”, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: Wrinkled wing skin is the most easily detected sign of an excessive load having been imposed during a landing. Another indication easily detected is fuel leakage along riveted seams.

notes.front: After flight through severe turbulence, where is inspection emphasis placed first?
notes.back: Upper and lower wing surfaces, for excessive buckles or wrinkles with permanent set.
notes.explanation: Where wrinkles have occurred, a few rivets are removed and their shanks examined for shear.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Severe Turbulence Inspection/Over “G””, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: Emphasis is placed upon inspecting the upper and lower wing surfaces for excessive buckles or wrinkles with permanent set.

notes.front: Through which structures does lightning current cause burning and more serious damage?
notes.back: Non-metallic ones, such as a fibreglass radome, cowl or fairing, windows, or composites without built-in bonding.
notes.explanation: Through good conductors such as aluminium or steel, damage is likely to be minimal or nonexistent.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lightning Strike”, p. 10-16
notes.evidence: When surges of high-voltage electricity pass through non-metallic structures, such as a fiberglass radome, engine cowl or fairing, glass or plastic window, or a composite structure that does not have built-in electrical bonding, burning and more serious damage to the structure could occur.

notes.front: Why may a fire-exposed structure with no visible damage still be unairworthy?
notes.back: Exposure to unusually high heat could severely degrade the design strength of heat-treated structural parts.
notes.explanation: Most structural metal components were heat-treated during manufacture.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fire Damage”, p. 10-16
notes.evidence: Since most structural metallic components of an aircraft have undergone some sort of heattreatment process during manufacture, an exposure to high heat not encountered during normal operations could severely degrade the design strength of the structure.

notes.front: Who generally specifies which nondestructive method and procedure to use?
notes.back: The product manufacturer or the Federal Aviation Administration.
notes.explanation: The requirements appear in manufacturers’ manuals, airworthiness directives, supplemental structural inspection documents or service bulletins.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Training, Qualification, & Certification”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: The product manufacturer or the FAA generally specifies the particular NDI method and procedure to be used in inspection.

notes.front: When may the handbook’s table of advantages and disadvantages be used to choose a nondestructive method?
notes.back: When neither the manufacturer nor the Federal Aviation Administration has specified a method.
notes.explanation: The table is a guide for evaluating the most appropriate method.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Advantages & Disadvantages of NDI Methods”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: This table could be used as a guide for evaluating the most appropriate NDI method when the manufacturer or the FAA has not specified a particular NDI method to be used.

notes.front: Before nondestructive inspection, what is generally needed for the part, and what for the equipment?
notes.back: The part thoroughly cleaned; the equipment’s calibration and inspection current, if required.
notes.explanation: Some parts must also be removed, or have paint or protective coating stripped.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “General Techniques”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: Generally, the parts or areas must be thoroughly cleaned. Some parts must be removed from the aircraft or engine. Others might need to have any paint or protective coating stripped. A complete knowledge of the equipment and procedures is essential and, if required, calibration and inspection of the equipment must be current.

notes.front: Under AC 43.13-1B’s NDT levels, what certificate must a Level I/Level II individual hold?
notes.back: An airframe and powerplant mechanic certificate.
notes.explanation: They must also complete the required formal classroom hours and an examination.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Acceptable Methods, Techniques, and Practices – Aircraft Inspection and Repair, “5-3. NDT Levels”, p. 5-1
notes.evidence: Level I/Level II. The individual shall have an FAA Airframe and Powerplant Mechanic Certificate, complete the required number of formal classroom hours, and complete an examination.

notes.front: With what three aids can a visual inspection be enhanced?
notes.back: A bright light, a magnifying glass and a mirror.
notes.explanation: Some defects lie beneath the surface or are too small for the eye, even magnified.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: Visual inspection can be enhanced by looking at the suspect area with a bright light, a magnifying glass, and a mirror.

notes.front: When searching for surface cracks with a flashlight, at what angle to the surface do you direct the beam?
notes.back: 5 to 45 degrees, towards the face.
notes.explanation: Keep your eyes above the reflected beam so it does not shine into them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cracks”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: When searching for surface cracks with a flashlight, direct the light beam at a 5 to 45 degree angle to the inspection surface towards the face.

notes.front: What magnifier does the handbook say to use to confirm a suspected crack?
notes.back: A 10-power magnifying glass.
notes.explanation: If that is not adequate, verify with other methods such as penetrant, magnetic particle or eddy current.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cracks”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: Use a 10-power magnifying glass to confirm the existence of a suspected crack. If this is not adequate, use other NDI techniques, such as penetrant, magnetic particle, or eddy current to verify cracks.

notes.front: What are the two basic borescope configurations?
notes.back: A rigid, small-diameter telescope with a tiny mirror at the end, and a flexible fibre-optic type.
notes.explanation: The mirror lets the user see around corners; fibre optics give greater flexibility.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Borescope”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: The simpler of the two is a rigid type, small diameter telescope with a tiny mirror at the end that enables the user to see around corners. The other type uses fiber optics that enable greater flexibility.

notes.front: What are two non-metal materials that penetrant inspection may also be used on?
notes.back: Any two of ceramics, plastics, molded rubber and glass.
notes.explanation: It works on any nonporous material, and on metals such as aluminium, magnesium, brass, copper, cast iron, stainless steel and titanium.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Liquid Penetrant Inspection”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: It is used with equal success on such metals as aluminum, magnesium, brass, copper, cast iron, stainless steel, and titanium. It may also be used on ceramics, plastics, molded rubber, and glass.

notes.front: What is the main disadvantage of penetrant inspection?
notes.back: The defect must be open to the surface for the penetrant to get in.
notes.explanation: For magnetic materials, magnetic particle inspection is therefore generally recommended.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Liquid Penetrant Inspection”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: The main disadvantage of penetrant inspection is that the defect must be open to the surface in order to let the penetrant get into the defect.

notes.front: In the six penetrant steps, what comes between applying the penetrant and drying the part?
notes.back: Removing the penetrant with remover emulsifier or cleaner.
notes.explanation: The full order is: clean, apply penetrant, remove it, dry, apply developer, inspect and interpret.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Liquid Penetrant Inspection”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: 1. Clean the metal surface thoroughly. 2. Apply penetrant. 3. Remove penetrant with remover emulsifier or cleaner. 4. Dry the part. 5. Apply the developer. 6. Inspect and interpret results.

notes.front: In penetrant inspection, how does defect size relate to penetrating time?
notes.back: The smaller the defect, the longer the penetrating time.
notes.explanation: Fine crack-like openings need longer than defects such as pores.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Interpretation of Results”, p. 10-19
notes.evidence: The smaller the defect, the longer the penetrating time. Fine crack-like apertures require a longer penetrating time than defects such as pores.

notes.front: With visible penetrant, what colour are defect indications against the developer?
notes.back: Bright red on a smooth white coating.
notes.explanation: If no red indications appear, there are no surface defects.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Interpretation of Results”, p. 10-19
notes.evidence: Visible penetrant-type developer, when applied to the surface of a part, dries to a smooth, white coating. As the developer dries, bright red indications appear where there are surface defects.

notes.front: Under black light in fluorescent penetrant inspection, what colours are defects and sound areas?
notes.back: Defects brilliant yellow-green; sound areas deep blue-violet.
notes.explanation: This is the fluorescent counterpart of the red-on-white visible method.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Interpretation of Results”, p. 10-19
notes.evidence: When conducting the fluorescent penetrant-type inspection, the defects show up (under black light) as a brilliant yellow-green color and the sound areas appear deep blue-violet.

notes.front: How do you recognise a false penetrant indication caused by poor washing?
notes.back: The penetrant lies in broad areas rather than the sharp patterns of true indications.
notes.explanation: The part must then be completely reprocessed; degreasing is recommended to remove all traces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “False Indications”, p. 10-20
notes.evidence: Evidences of incomplete washing are usually easy to identify since the penetrant is in broad areas rather than in the sharp patterns found with true indications.

notes.front: Why does penetrant show an indication where a wheel is press fit onto a shaft?
notes.back: The two parts are not welded together, so the fit line holds penetrant; this is perfectly normal.
notes.explanation: Such indications are easy to identify because they are regular in form and shape.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “False Indications”, p. 10-20
notes.evidence: If a wheel is press fit onto a shaft, penetrant shows an indication at the fit line. This is perfectly normal since the two parts are not meant to be welded together.

notes.front: What are two things eddy current inspection is used to detect or determine?
notes.back: Any two of surface cracks, pits, subsurface cracks, corrosion on inner surfaces, and alloy and heat-treat condition.
notes.explanation: In maintenance it inspects turbine shafts and vanes, wing skins, wheels, bolt holes and spark plug bores.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Eddy Current Inspection”, p. 10-20
notes.evidence: Eddy current is used to detect surface cracks, pits, subsurface cracks, corrosion on inner surfaces, and to determine alloy and heat-treat condition.

notes.front: Must primer, paint and anodised films usually be removed for eddy current inspection?
notes.back: No: it can frequently be performed without removing surface coatings.
notes.explanation: It can be effective in detecting surface and subsurface corrosion and heat-treat condition.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Principles of Operations”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: Eddy current inspection can frequently be performed without removing the surface coatings, such as primer, paint, and anodized films.

notes.front: For eddy current calibration, what must the reference standard be made from?
notes.back: The same material as the item to be tested.
notes.explanation: It contains known flaws, such as a surface notch, fastener hole or countersink hole.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Eddy Current Instruments”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: A reference standard is required for the calibration of eddy current test equipment. A reference standard is made from the same material as the item is to be tested.

notes.front: What are the three basic ultrasonic inspection methods?
notes.back: Pulse echo, through-transmission and resonance.
notes.explanation: Each detects flaws differently: by reflected echoes, by a disrupted sound path, or by varying frequency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Ultrasonic Inspection”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: There are three basic ultrasonic inspection methods: pulse echo, through-transmission, and resonance.

notes.front: How does the pulse echo method detect flaws?
notes.back: By measuring the amplitude of reflected signals and the time they take to travel between surfaces and the discontinuity.
notes.explanation: The reflected pulse is displayed in the same relation to front and back pulses as the flaw is to the surfaces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Pulse Echo”, p. 10-22
notes.evidence: Flaws are detected by measuring the amplitude of signals reflected and the time required for these signals to travel between specific surfaces and the discontinuity.

notes.front: How many transducers does through-transmission use, and where?
notes.back: Two: one generates the pulse and another on the opposite surface receives it.
notes.explanation: A disruption in the sound path indicates a flaw; the method is less sensitive to small defects than pulse echo.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Through-Transmission”, p. 10-23
notes.evidence: Through-transmission inspection uses two transducers, one to generate the pulse and another placed on the opposite surface

notes.front: What is the ultrasonic resonance method used principally for?
notes.back: Thickness measurement when both sides are smooth and parallel and the back is inaccessible.
notes.explanation: Unlike pulse methods, it continuously varies the transmission frequency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Resonance”, p. 10-25
notes.evidence: measurements when the two sides of the material being tested are smooth and parallel and the backside is inaccessible.

notes.front: How many surfaces of the material does an ultrasonic test instrument need access to?
notes.back: Only one.
notes.explanation: It can use straight line or angle beam techniques, and finds cracks and voids too small for X-ray.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Ultrasonic Inspection”, p. 10-21
notes.evidence: An ultrasonic test instrument requires access to only one surface of the material to be inspected and can be used with either straight line or angle beam testing techniques.

notes.front: What two purposes do ultrasonic reference standards serve?
notes.back: A response pattern related to the part inspected, and the required inspection sensitivity.
notes.explanation: The standard holds a simulated defect, a notch, sized to set sensitivity to the expected defect.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Reference Standards”, p. 10-26
notes.evidence: Reference standards serve two purposes: to provide an ultrasonic response pattern that is related to the part being inspected and to establish the required inspection sensitivity.

notes.front: In the five types of bonded-structure defect, what is a Type V defect?
notes.back: Water in the core.
notes.explanation: Type I, by contrast, is disbonds or voids at an outer skin-to-adhesive interface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Defects”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: 5. Type V—water in the core.

notes.front: What advantage does acoustic emission testing have over other nondestructive methods?
notes.back: It can detect and locate all of the activated flaws in a structure in one test.
notes.explanation: The bursts can also be used to evaluate flaw growth rate as a function of applied stress.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Acoustic Emission Inspection”, p. 10-28
notes.evidence: can detect and locate all of the activated flaws in a structure

notes.front: In magnetic particle inspection, what is an “indication”?
notes.back: The particle pattern that forms between opposite poles at a discontinuity, taking its approximate surface shape.
notes.explanation: A discontinuity disturbs the magnetic lines of force, creating poles on either side.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnetic Particle Inspection”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: The magnetized particles thus form a pattern in the magnetic field between the opposite poles. This pattern, known as an “indication,” assumes the approximate shape of the surface projection of the discontinuity.

notes.front: To locate a defect, how must the magnetic lines of force run relative to it?
notes.back: Approximately perpendicular to the defect.
notes.explanation: Defects can lie at any angle, so flux is induced in more than one direction by two separate magnetising operations.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Effect of Flux Direction”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: To locate a defect in a part, it is essential that the magnetic lines of force pass approximately perpendicular to the defect.

notes.front: How is circular magnetisation produced, and which defects does it locate?
notes.back: By passing current through the part; it locates defects running approximately parallel to the part’s axis.
notes.explanation: The field forms concentric circles of force about and within the part.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Effect of Flux Direction”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: This is achieved by passing electric current through the part, locating defects running approximately parallel to the axis of the part.

notes.front: How is longitudinal magnetisation produced, and in which direction is its field?
notes.back: By placing the part in a solenoid; the field runs parallel to the part’s long axis.
notes.explanation: The part becomes the core of an electromagnet, magnetised by induction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Effect of Flux Direction”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: the magnetic field is produced in a direction parallel to the long axis of the part. This is accomplished by placing the part in a solenoid excited by electric current.

notes.front: What problem do excessively high flux densities cause in magnetic particle inspection?
notes.back: Nonrelevant indications, such as patterns of grain flow, that interfere with finding significant discontinuities.
notes.explanation: So the field must be strong enough to reveal harmful discontinuities but not strong enough to confuse.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Effect of Flux Density”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: Excessively high flux densities may form nonrelevant indications, such as patterns of the grain flow in the material.

notes.front: In the continuous method, when is the indicating medium applied?
notes.back: While the magnetising force is maintained.
notes.explanation: The available flux density is then at its maximum.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnetizing Methods”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: In the continuous inspection method, the part is magnetized and the indicating medium applied while the magnetizing force is maintained.

notes.front: What is the mixing ratio of Magnaglo paste in light oil?
notes.back: 0.10 to 0.25 ounce of paste per gallon of oil.
notes.explanation: After inspection the part must be demagnetised and rinsed with a cleaning solvent.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnaglo Inspection”, p. 10-32
notes.evidence: The reddishbrown liquid spray or bath that is used consists of Magnaglo paste mixed with a light oil at the ratio of 0.10 to 0.25 ounce of paste per gallon of oil.

notes.front: Why must parts of operating mechanisms be demagnetised?
notes.back: So they do not attract filings, chips or wear particles, which may score bearings or other working parts.
notes.explanation: Airframe parts are demagnetised so they do not affect instruments.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Demagnetizing”, p. 10-33
notes.evidence: Parts of operating mechanisms must be demagnetized to prevent magnetized parts from attracting filings, grindings, or chips inadvertently left in the system or steel particles resulting from operational wear.

notes.front: What kind of magnetising force demagnetises an aircraft part?
notes.back: One that keeps reversing direction while gradually decreasing in strength.
notes.explanation: As the force alternates and falls, the part’s magnetisation decreases too.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Demagnetizing”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: A convenient procedure for aircraft parts involves subjecting the part to a magnetizing force that is continually reversing in direction and, at the same time, gradually decreasing in strength.

notes.front: When withdrawing a part from an AC demagnetising coil, how far away should it be before the current is cut off?
notes.back: 1 or 2 feet from the opening.
notes.explanation: Cutting the current too soon may remagnetise the part.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Standard Demagnetizing Practice”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: The demagnetizing current is not cut off until the part is 1 or 2 feet from the opening as the part may be remagnetized if current is removed too soon.

notes.front: How much disassembly does radiographic inspection need?
notes.back: Little or none.
notes.explanation: Other nondestructive methods usually need removal, disassembly and paint stripping first.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Radiographic Inspection”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: Radiographic inspection techniques are used to locate defects or flaws in airframe structures or engines with little or no disassembly.

notes.front: What are the three major steps in the X-ray process?
notes.back: Exposure to radiation (including preparation), processing of film, and interpretation of the radiograph.
notes.explanation: Only qualified radiographers may operate X-ray units.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Radiographic Inspection”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: Three major steps in the x-ray process discussed in subsequent paragraphs are: exposure to radiation, including preparation; processing of film; and interpretation of the radiograph.

notes.front: Which phase does the handbook call the most important in radiography, from a quality-assurance standpoint?
notes.back: Radiographic interpretation.
notes.explanation: It is where the part is accepted or rejected, and where an error in judgement can have disastrous consequences.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Radiographic Interpretation”, p. 10-35
notes.evidence: From the standpoint of quality assurance, radiographic interpretation is the most important phase of radiography.

notes.front: Where must personnel keep in relation to an X-ray unit’s primary beam?
notes.back: Outside it at all times.
notes.explanation: Radiation from X-ray units and radioisotope sources is destructive to living tissue.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Radiation Hazards”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: Radiation from x-ray units and radioisotope sources is destructive to living tissue. It is universally recognized that in the use of such equipment, adequate protection must be provided. Personnel must keep outside the primary x-ray beam at all times.

notes.front: For what are composite structures inspected?
notes.back: Delamination, debonding of skin from core, and evidence of moisture and corrosion.
notes.explanation: Delamination means separation of the plies.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Inspection of Composites”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: Composite structures are inspected for delamination (separation of the various plies), debonding of the skin from the core, and evidence of moisture and corrosion.

notes.front: In a tap test, what is the maximum weight of the hammer?
notes.back: 2 ounces.
notes.explanation: A coin or other suitable device may be used instead of the light hammer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Tap Testing”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: The testing procedure consists of lightly tapping the surface with a light weight hammer (maximum weight of 2 ounces), a coin, or other suitable device.

notes.front: In a tap test, what response indicates an area of concern?
notes.back: A “flat” or “dead” response, compared with the ring of a known good area.
notes.explanation: The acoustic response is always compared with a known good area.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Tap Testing”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: The acoustic response or “ring” is compared to that of a known good area. A “flat” or “dead” response indicates an area of concern.

notes.front: Tap testing is limited to finding defects in relatively thin skins, less than {{c1::0.080}} inch thick.
notes.back: 0.080 inch.
notes.explanation: Thicker laminates need other methods recommended by the manufacturer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Tap Testing”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: Tap testing is limited to finding defects in relatively thin skins, less than 0.080" thick.

notes.front: A common screwdriver must fill at least {{c1::75}} percent of the screw slot.
notes.back: 75 percent.
notes.explanation: A wrong-size blade cuts and burrs the slot and may slip and damage nearby structure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Screwdrivers”, p. 11-1
notes.evidence: A common screwdriver must fill at least 75 percent of the screw slot.

notes.front: On an adjustable wrench, to which side of the handle do you always apply the pull?
notes.back: The side attached to the fixed jaw.
notes.explanation: Fitting the wrench carefully also reduces the chance of rounding off the fastener.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Wrenches”, p. 11-5
notes.evidence: When using any adjustable wrench, always exert the pull on the side of the handle attached to the fixed jaw of the wrench.

notes.front: What calibration intervals may torque wrenches or tools recommend?
notes.back: Six months for some, twelve months for others.
notes.explanation: Intervals depend on the tool, and regular calibration keeps it accurate; note the handbook elsewhere (p. 7-49) says to test torque wrenches at least once a month.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Torque Wrench”, p. 11-6
notes.evidence: Some wrenches or tools may recommend six (6) month calibration intervals, while others may schedule it at twelve (12) months.

notes.front: Which hacksaw blade pitch is used for thin-walled tubing and sheet metal?
notes.back: 32 teeth per inch.
notes.explanation: Pitches of 14, 18, 24 and 32 teeth per inch are available.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Hacksaws”, p. 11-8
notes.evidence: Use the 32 teeth per inch blade for cutting thin-walled tubing and sheet metal.

notes.front: What cutting angle does a twist drill need for most drilling, and what may be better for soft metals?
notes.back: 118° (59° either side of centre); 90° may be more efficient for soft metals.
notes.explanation: The drill should be sharpened at the first sign of dullness.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Twist Drills”, p. 11-12
notes.evidence: For most drilling, a twist drill with a cutting angle of 118° (59° on either side of center) is sufficient. However, when drilling soft metals, a cutting angle of 90° may be more efficient.

notes.front: How far undersize should a hole be drilled before it is reamed to exact size?
notes.back: About 0.003 to 0.007 inch.
notes.explanation: Removing more than 0.007 inch places too much load on the reamer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Reamers”, p. 11-13
notes.evidence: A hole that is to be reamed to exact size must be drilled about 0.003 to 0.007 inch undersize.

notes.front: What is the smallest measurement you can make with a steel rule?
notes.back: One sixty-fourth of an inch in common fractions; one hundredth in decimal fractions.
notes.explanation: Closer measurement needs a micrometer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Micrometer Calipers”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: The smallest measurement that can be made with the use of the steel rule is one sixty-fourth of an inch in common fractions and one one-hundredth of an inch in decimal fractions.

notes.front: On a combination set, what are the centre head and the protractor head used for?
notes.back: The centre head finds the centre of shafts; the protractor head checks angles or draws lines at a set angle.
notes.explanation: The stock head carries the level and scriber.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Combination Sets”, p. 11-18
notes.evidence: The center head is used to find the center of shafts or other cylindrical work. The protractor head can be used to check angles and also may be set at any desired angle to draw lines.

notes.front: What are the four types of micrometer calipers?
notes.back: Outside, inside, depth and thread micrometers.
notes.explanation: All four are read in the same way; the outside micrometer is used most.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Micrometer Calipers”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: There are four types of micrometer calipers, each designed for a specific use: outside micrometer, inside micrometer, depth micrometer, and thread micrometer.

notes.front: What are the fixed parts of a micrometer?
notes.back: The frame, barrel and anvil.
notes.explanation: The movable parts are the thimble and spindle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Micrometer Parts”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: The fixed parts of a micrometer are the frame, barrel, and anvil.

notes.front: What are the movable parts of a micrometer, and how do they work together?
notes.back: The thimble and spindle: the thimble rotates the spindle, which moves in the threaded part inside the barrel.
notes.explanation: The work is measured in the opening between anvil and spindle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Micrometer Parts”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: The movable parts of a micrometer are the thimble and spindle. The thimble rotates the spindle, which moves in the threaded portion inside the barrel.

notes.front: On a micrometer barrel, each tenth is divided into four parts of {{c1::0.025}} inch each.
notes.back: 0.025 inch.
notes.explanation: One complete revolution of the thimble moves it one of these divisions along the barrel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Reading a Micrometer”, p. 11-22
notes.evidence: Each of the sections between the tenths divisions (between 1, 2, 3, 4, and so forth) is divided into four parts of 0.025 inch each.

notes.front: How many divisions has a micrometer thimble’s bevel edge, and what is each worth?
notes.back: 25 divisions, each 0.001 inch.
notes.explanation: Each is one twenty-fifth of the 0.025 inch the thimble travels in one revolution.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Reading a Micrometer”, p. 11-22
notes.evidence: The bevel edge of the thimble is divided into 25 equal parts.

notes.front: What establishes the 0.025 inch barrel graduations of a micrometer?
notes.back: The lead screw, with 40 threads per inch.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives this as an excellent way to remember the scale values.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Vernier Scale”, p. 11-23
notes.evidence: an excellent way to remember the relative scale values is to remember that the 0.025 inch barrel scale graduations are established by the lead screw (40 threads per inch).

notes.front: Which vernier line do you read on a micrometer?
notes.back: The one aligned exactly with any thimble graduation.
notes.explanation: The vernier reading is added last, after the barrel and thimble readings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Vernier Scale”, p. 11-23
notes.evidence: The vernier scale line to be read is always the one aligned exactly with

notes.front: What may happen if a micrometer is dropped?
notes.back: Its accuracy may be permanently affected.
notes.explanation: Overtightening the spindle may also spring the frame permanently and give inaccurate readings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Using a Micrometer”, p. 11-24
notes.evidence: The micrometer must be handled carefully. If it is dropped, its accuracy may be permanently affected.

notes.front: What are two types of gauge used when calibrating a micrometer, following the manufacturer’s instructions?
notes.back: Any two of gauge blocks, gauge pins and ring gauges.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to follow the manufacturer’s instructions for calibration procedures in any event.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Using a Micrometer”, p. 11-24
notes.evidence: In any event, follow the manufacturer’s instructions for calibration procedures and types of gauges to be used, such as gauge blocks, gauge pins, or ring gauges.

notes.front: When using a dial indicator, why must it be securely fastened?
notes.back: So that movement of the indicator itself induces no errors in measurement.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls this imperative, whether the part or an installed brake disc is checked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Using a Micrometer”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: it is imperative that the dial indicator be securely fastened so that movement of the indicator itself induces no errors in measurement.

notes.front: When checking a shaft with a dial indicator, what is the runout?
notes.back: The total amount the needle fluctuates as the part is rotated.
notes.explanation: The dial is zeroed first, with the probe lightly contacting the surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Using a Micrometer”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: The part is then rotated, and the amount of bend, or run out, is displayed on the dial as the needle fluctuates. The total amount of the fluctuation is the runout.

notes.front: What can a slide caliper measure that a ruler cannot, thanks to its specially formed jaws?
notes.back: Both inside and outside dimensions, with greater accuracy than a ruler.
notes.explanation: Some also contain a depth gauge for blind holes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Slide Calipers”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: Often used to measure the length of an object, the slide caliper provides greater accuracy than the ruler. It can, by virtue of its specially formed jaws, measure both inside and outside dimensions.

notes.front: Why must a resistor be disconnected from its circuit before you check it with an ohmmeter?
notes.back: To prevent possible damage to the ohmmeter and inaccurate readings from parallel circuit paths.
notes.explanation: The ACS lists damage prevention when using an ohmmeter as a risk element.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Checking Resistance in a Circuit”, p. 12-81
notes.evidence: To check the value of a resistor, the resistor must be disconnected from the circuit. This prevents any possible damage to the ohmmeter, and it prevents the possibility of any inaccurate readings

notes.front: When an ohmmeter is used on a circuit, what two conditions must the tested component meet?
notes.back: It must be isolated, and the power source removed from the circuit.
notes.explanation: In the handbook’s example, opening the circuit switch meets both.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Tracing Opens with the Ohmmeter”, p. 12-82
notes.evidence: When an ohmmeter is used, the circuit component to be tested must be isolated and the power source removed from the circuit.

notes.front: A technician removes the cowling for an inspection and sees fresh oil streaks. The cowl area is dirty. What should they do before cleaning it?
notes.back: C: Take note of the oil or fluid leakage.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to note any oil or other evidence of fluid leakage before cleaning, since cleaning would erase it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Basic Inspection Techniques/Practices”, p. 10-1
notes.evidence: When opening inspection plates and cowling, and before cleaning the area, take note of any oil or other evidence of fluid leakage.
notes.choices:
A) Clean first so the structure can be seen
B) Close the cowling and ground run the engine
C) Take note of the oil or fluid leakage
D) Skip the area; it is outside the checklist
notes.choicesExplained: A would wipe away the leak evidence. B is not a step the handbook gives here. D ignores a finding and the rule to open and clean all areas.

notes.front: A mechanic has done dozens of inspections on one aircraft type and is sure they know every item. What does the handbook say about using a checklist?
notes.back: A: Always use a checklist when performing an inspection.
notes.explanation: The rule is unconditional: a checklist makes sure no items are forgotten or overlooked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Checklists”, p. 10-2
notes.evidence: Always use a checklist when performing an inspection.
notes.choices:
A) Always use a checklist when performing an inspection
B) Use one only for annual inspections
C) Experienced mechanics may work from memory
D) Use the pilot’s preflight checklist instead
notes.choicesExplained: C and B add exceptions the handbook does not make. D is the pilot’s checklist, not an inspection checklist.

notes.front: Before a morning flight, the pilot walks around the aeroplane checking its general condition and checks fuel and oil levels. What is this?
notes.back: A: A preflight inspection.
notes.explanation: The pilot’s checklist section “Preflight Inspection” includes the walk-around and fluid checks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Preflight/Postflight Inspections”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: The preflight inspection checklist includes a “walk-around” section listing items that the pilot is to visually check for general condition as they walk around the airplane.
notes.choices:
A) A preflight inspection
B) A 100-hour inspection
C) A conformity check
D) A special inspection
notes.choicesExplained: B is a complete inspection by a certificated technician. C checks equipment against the type certificate data sheet. D follows an unusual event such as a hard landing.

notes.front: A privately used aeroplane is due its annual inspection. The only mechanic available holds an airframe and powerplant certificate but no inspection authorisation. What follows?
notes.back: D: They may not; an annual needs a technician holding inspection authorisation.
notes.explanation: Scope is identical, but one difference is who may do it: annual inspections need an airframe and powerplant technician with inspection authorisation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Annual/100-Hour Inspections”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: A certified airframe and powerplant (A&P) maintenance technician can conduct a 100-hour inspection, whereas an annual inspection must be conducted by a certified A&P maintenance technician with inspection authorization (IA).
notes.choices:
A) They may do it, as the scope equals a 100-hour
B) They may do it if the aeroplane is flown under 100 hours a year
C) They may do only the progressive phases
D) They may not; an annual needs a technician holding inspection authorisation
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses scope with authority. B invents a usage exception. C is a different programme with its own approval.

notes.front: An air taxi operator wants its aircraft inspected in segments, finishing each one overnight so the aircraft can still fly every day. Which programme fits?
notes.back: B: A progressive inspection programme.
notes.explanation: A progressive programme splits the annual inspection into phases, and any phase can be done overnight so revenue flying continues.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Progressive Inspections”, p. 10-12
notes.evidence: The advantage of such a program is that any required segment may be completed overnight and thus enable the aircraft to fly daily without missing any revenue earning potential.
notes.choices:
A) A calendar-only annual inspection
B) A progressive inspection programme
C) A special inspection after each flight
D) An altimeter and transponder check
notes.choicesExplained: A keeps the whole inspection in one long block. C is for unusual events. D covers only instruments.

notes.front: After a firm arrival well below the maximum design landing weight, the crew report a “bang”. What does the handbook say about a special inspection?
notes.back: B: Performed after a rough landing even when the design landing weight was not exceeded.
notes.explanation: Vertical velocity at touchdown is hard to estimate, so a rough landing gets a special inspection whatever the weight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Hard or Overweight Landing Inspection”, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: a special inspection is performed after a landing is made at a weight known to exceed the design landing weight or after a rough landing, even though the latter may have occurred when the aircraft did not exceed the design landing weight.
notes.choices:
A) Not needed, because the weight was below the limit
B) Performed after a rough landing even when the design landing weight was not exceeded
C) Needed only if a tyre has burst
D) Needed only after the next 100 hours
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that severity of impact, not just weight, causes stress. C and D add conditions the handbook does not give.

notes.front: A steel engine mount was near a hangar fire. It shows no visible damage but its strength is in doubt. Which check does the handbook suggest?
notes.back: A: A hardness test, such as a Rockwell C tester.
notes.explanation: Strength of metals is related to hardness, so a hardness tester can reveal damage to steel structures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fire Damage”, p. 10-16
notes.evidence: Since strength of metals is related to hardness, possible damage to steel structures might be determined by use of a hardness tester, such as a Rockwell C hardness tester.
notes.choices:
A) A hardness test, such as a Rockwell C tester
B) An eddy current conductivity test only
C) A tap test with a coin
D) A borescope inspection
notes.choicesExplained: B is the handbook’s suggestion for aluminium. C is for thin composite skins. D is visual and cannot measure strength.

notes.front: After severe turbulence you find a sizeable fuel leak along a wing seam. What does it suggest?
notes.back: A: The area may have received overloads that broke the sealant and opened the seams.
notes.explanation: The handbook reads a sizeable leak after turbulence as a sign of overload in that area.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Severe Turbulence Inspection/Over “G””, p. 10-15
notes.evidence: Any sizeable fuel leak is an indication that an area may have received overloads that have broken the sealant and opened the seams.
notes.choices:
A) The area may have received overloads that broke the sealant and opened the seams
B) Only a loose fuel cap
C) A failed fuel pump
D) Normal seepage that needs no action
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C ignore that the leak follows a structural overload event.

notes.front: A close visual check of a highly stressed fitting shows no defects. Can the technician conclude no further inspection is needed?
notes.back: D: No, defects may be beneath the surface or too small to see.
notes.explanation: The lack of visible defects does not necessarily mean further inspection is unnecessary.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Visual Inspection”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: The lack of visible defects does not necessarily mean further inspection is unnecessary. Some defects may lie beneath the surface or may be so small that the human eye, even with the assistance of a magnifying glass, cannot detect them.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, a clean visual check proves the part sound
B) No, visual inspection is never allowed on fittings
C) Yes, if a mirror was used
D) No, defects may be beneath the surface or too small to see
notes.choicesExplained: A and C overstate what the eye can find, even with aids. B invents a ban.

notes.front: You suspect a cracked cylinder in a reciprocating engine and want to look inside without tearing it down. Which tool fits?
notes.back: C: A borescope.
notes.explanation: Borescopes are typically used to search for cracked cylinders in reciprocating engines without disassembly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Borescope”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: search for cracked cylinders in aircraft reciprocating engines; inspect turbojet engine turbine blades and combustion cans;
notes.choices:
A) A dial indicator
B) A combination set
C) A borescope
D) A hermaphrodite caliper
notes.choicesExplained: A measures surface variation. B is a layout tool. D is a marking gauge.

notes.front: A steel part must be checked for cracks, and magnetic particle equipment is available. What does the handbook say about using penetrant?
notes.back: D: Magnetic particle inspection should be used for a material susceptible to magnetism.
notes.explanation: The handbook says a part made of a material susceptible to magnetism should be inspected by a magnetic particle method if equipment is available.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Interpretation of Results”, p. 10-19
notes.evidence: When the part to be inspected is made of a material susceptible to magnetism, it should be inspected by a magnetic particle inspection method if the equipment is available.
notes.choices:
A) Penetrant is always preferred on steel
B) Use penetrant, then radiography
C) Neither method works on steel
D) Magnetic particle inspection should be used for a material susceptible to magnetism
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the guidance. C is wrong: magnetic particle works on ferromagnetic steel. B is not given.

notes.front: After an aggressive rinse, a penetrant check of a part known to be cracked shows nothing. What is the likeliest reason?
notes.back: D: All the penetrant was washed out of the defect.
notes.explanation: If all penetrant is washed out of a defect, no indication can form; rinsing can remove it from inside the defect as well as the surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Interpretation of Results”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: If all penetrant is washed out of a defect, an indication cannot be formed.
notes.choices:
A) The developer was too white
B) The part was too clean
C) Penetrant never shows fatigue cracks
D) All the penetrant was washed out of the defect
notes.choicesExplained: A is normal. B helps the penetrant enter. C is wrong: fatigue cracks are among the defects it detects.

notes.front: An aluminium bolt hole in a painted wing skin must be checked for subsurface cracks without stripping the paint. Which method fits best?
notes.back: A: Eddy current inspection.
notes.explanation: Eddy current finds surface and subsurface cracks in conductive metals and often works through paint.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Eddy Current Inspection”, p. 10-20
notes.evidence: Eddy current is used in aircraft maintenance to inspect jet engine turbine shafts and vanes, wing skins, wheels, bolt holes, and spark plug bores for cracks, heat, or frame damage.
notes.choices:
A) Eddy current inspection
B) Magnetic particle inspection
C) Visible dye penetrant
D) Tap test
notes.choicesExplained: B needs ferromagnetic material. C needs a surface opening, so paint must come off. D is for composite delamination.

notes.front: You must find a small internal flaw in a thick part and can reach only one surface. Which method suits?
notes.back: C: Pulse echo ultrasonic.
notes.explanation: Pulse echo works from one surface by timing reflections, and through-transmission is less sensitive to small defects and needs the opposite side.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Through-Transmission”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: Through-transmission is less sensitive to small defects than the pulse-echo method.
notes.choices:
A) Through-transmission ultrasonic
B) Visual inspection with a mirror
C) Pulse echo ultrasonic
D) Resonance with both sides accessible
notes.choicesExplained: A needs a transducer on each side. B cannot see inside. D contradicts the scenario, since only one side can be reached, and resonance is used mainly to measure thickness, not to find small flaws.

notes.front: A trainee presses an ultrasonic transducer onto a dry panel and gets no useful signal. What is missing?
notes.back: B: A couplant layer.
notes.explanation: Ultrasonic energy does not travel through air, so a couplant must join transducer and test piece.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Couplants”, p. 10-26
notes.evidence: Inspection with ultrasonics is limited to the part in contact with the transducer.
notes.choices:
A) A black light
B) A couplant layer
C) A reference standard notch
D) Demagnetisation
notes.choicesExplained: A is for fluorescent methods. C calibrates but does not carry sound. D belongs to magnetic particle work.

notes.front: A technician proposes magnetic particle inspection of an aluminium wheel half. What is wrong?
notes.back: A: Aluminium is nonmagnetic, so the method is not applicable.
notes.explanation: Magnetic particle inspection works only on ferromagnetic materials such as iron and steel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnetic Particle Inspection”, p. 10-29
notes.evidence: Magnetic particle inspection is a method of detecting invisible cracks and other defects in ferromagnetic materials, such as iron and steel. It is not applicable to nonmagnetic materials.
notes.choices:
A) Aluminium is nonmagnetic, so the method is not applicable
B) Aluminium needs the residual method
C) The wheel must first be heated
D) Nothing; it is the preferred method
notes.choicesExplained: B and C invent workarounds. D contradicts the handbook.

notes.front: You suspect a crack running along the length of a steel shaft, parallel to its axis. Which magnetisation shows it?
notes.back: B: Circular, passing current through the part.
notes.explanation: Circular magnetisation locates defects running approximately parallel to the part’s axis, because the flux must cross the defect.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Effect of Flux Direction”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: Circular magnetization is the induction of a magnetic field consisting of concentric circles of force about and within the part.
notes.choices:
A) Longitudinal, with the part in a solenoid
B) Circular, passing current through the part
C) Neither; such cracks cannot be found
D) Demagnetising current only
notes.choicesExplained: A puts the field parallel to the crack. C is wrong. D removes magnetism rather than revealing defects.

notes.front: A critical steel part must be checked for subsurface discontinuities. Which magnetising procedure gives greater sensitivity?
notes.back: B: Continuous.
notes.explanation: The continuous procedure gives greater sensitivity than the residual one, particularly for subsurface discontinuities.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnetizing Methods”, p. 10-31
