notes.evidence: The continuous procedure provides greater sensitivity than the residual procedure, particularly in locating subsurface discontinuities.
notes.choices:
A) Residual
B) Continuous
C) Either; they are equal
D) Flexible coil residual only
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are less sensitive. C ignores the stated difference.

notes.front: After magnetic particle inspection, a crankshaft sits in the energised demagnetising coil for five minutes, then the current is switched off with it still inside. What is wrong?
notes.back: C: Leaving it in achieves little; it must be slowly withdrawn to 1 or 2 feet before cut-off.
notes.explanation: The effective operation is slowly moving the part out of the coil; staying in with current on does very little.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Standard Demagnetizing Practice”, p. 10-34
notes.evidence: Allowing a part to remain in the demagnetizer with the current on accomplishes very little practical demagnetization.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; time in the coil is what counts
B) The coil should use direct current
C) Leaving it in achieves little; it must be slowly withdrawn to 1 or 2 feet before cut-off
D) Crankshafts need no demagnetising
notes.choicesExplained: A contradicts the handbook. B is wrong: standard practice uses an AC coil. D ignores that operating parts must be demagnetised.

notes.front: An engine structure must be checked for internal flaws with little or no disassembly, and a permanent record is wanted. Which method fits?
notes.back: A: Radiography.
notes.explanation: Radiography finds flaws in structures or engines with little or no disassembly, and the handbook’s table lists a permanent test record.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Advantages & Disadvantages of NDI Methods”, p. 10-19
notes.evidence: Detects surface and internal flaws • Can inspect hidden areas X-Ray • Permanent test record obtained
notes.choices:
A) Radiography
B) Tap test
C) Visual inspection
D) Visible dye penetrant
notes.choicesExplained: B is for thin composite skins. C and D find only surface defects.

notes.front: During an X-ray exposure in the hangar, a colleague wants to stand near the unit to watch. What rule applies?
notes.back: A: Personnel must keep outside the primary beam at all times.
notes.explanation: Radiation is destructive to living tissue, so personnel must keep outside the primary X-ray beam at all times.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Radiation Hazards”, p. 10-36
notes.evidence: Personnel must keep outside the primary x-ray beam at all times.
notes.choices:
A) Personnel must keep outside the primary beam at all times
B) Allowed for short exposures
C) Allowed if wearing gloves
D) Allowed if the film is facing away
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D weaken an absolute rule.

notes.front: A technician tap tests one side of a thin honeycomb panel and finds a good ring everywhere. Is the panel cleared?
notes.back: A: No, both sides must be tested.
notes.explanation: Tapping one side would not detect debonding on the opposite side of honeycomb.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Tap Testing”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: On honeycomb structures, both sides need to be tested. Tap testing on one side alone would not detect debonding on the opposite side.
notes.choices:
A) No, both sides must be tested
B) Yes, if a coin was used
C) No, the panel needs radiography first
D) Yes, a good ring clears the whole panel
notes.choicesExplained: D and B ignore the far skin. C is not the rule the handbook gives.

notes.front: Which pairing of defect and method matches the handbook?
notes.back: A: Surface crack in any nonporous part: penetrant.
notes.explanation: Penetrant finds defects open to the surface in any nonporous material.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Liquid Penetrant Inspection”, p. 10-18
notes.evidence: Penetrant inspection detects defects, such as surface cracks or porosity.
notes.choices:
A) Surface crack in any nonporous part: penetrant
B) Surface crack in aluminium: magnetic particle
C) Composite delamination: magnetic particle
D) Subsurface crack in titanium: penetrant
notes.choicesExplained: C and B need ferromagnetic material. D fails because penetrant finds only surface-open defects.

notes.front: A thin composite laminate may have water ingress near the surface. You have a heat lamp and an infrared camera. Which method is this?
notes.back: B: Thermography.
notes.explanation: Thermography maps surface temperatures as heat flows; it is most effective for thin laminates or defects near the surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Thermography”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: Thermal methods are most effective for thin laminates or for defects near the surface.
notes.choices:
A) Magnaglo inspection
B) Thermography
C) Radiography
D) Pulse echo
notes.choicesExplained: A needs ferromagnetic parts. C and D use radiation and sound, not heat.

notes.front: A damaged section of a carbon fibre panel with an embedded copper mesh is repaired. What must the repair also restore?
notes.back: A: The continuity of the electrical path, including conductive material in the repair.
notes.explanation: The conductive path must be restored, from the original conductor to the replacement and back.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrical Conductivity”, p. 10-37
notes.evidence: Not only is it necessary to include the conductive material in the repair, but the continuity of the electrical path from the original conductive material to the replacement conductor and back to the original must be maintained.
notes.choices:
A) The continuity of the electrical path, including conductive material in the repair
B) The panel’s magnetism
C) A fluorescent coating
D) Nothing beyond the plies
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are unrelated. D leaves the conductive path broken.

notes.front: You must cut full threads right to the bottom of a blind hole. Which tap finishes the job?
notes.back: C: Bottoming tap.
notes.explanation: The bottoming tap is not tapered and cuts full threads to the bottom of a blind hole.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Taps and Dies”, p. 11-14
notes.evidence: The bottoming tap is not tapered. It is used to cut full threads to the bottom of a blind hole.
notes.choices:
A) Taper tap
B) Plug tap
C) Bottoming tap
D) A die
notes.choicesExplained: A starts the thread. B supplements the taper tap in thick stock. D cuts external threads.

notes.front: You need to find the centre of the end of a round bar. Which part of a combination set do you use?
notes.back: D: Centre head.
notes.explanation: The centre head finds the centre of shafts and other cylindrical work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Combination Sets”, p. 11-18
notes.evidence: The center head is used to find the center of shafts or other cylindrical work.
notes.choices:
A) Stock head
B) Protractor head
C) Scriber alone
D) Centre head
notes.choicesExplained: A squares and levels. B checks angles. C marks lines but finds no centre.

notes.front: A micrometer barrel shows the 3 line plus two 0.025 inch graduations, and thimble line 12 meets the horizontal line. What is the reading?
notes.back: D: 0.362 inch.
notes.explanation: Add the three figures: 0.300 + 0.050 + 0.012 = 0.362 inch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Reading a Micrometer”, p. 11-23
notes.evidence: Add to this the number of divisions on the bevel edge of the thimble that coincides with the line of the graduation. The total of the three figures equals the measurement.
notes.choices:
A) 0.312 inch
B) 0.3512 inch
C) 0.350 inch
D) 0.362 inch
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves out the two barrel graduations. C leaves out the thimble. B treats the thimble as ten-thousandths.

notes.front: A micrometer reads 0.425 inch on the barrel and 0.008 on the thimble, and vernier line 6 lines up exactly with a thimble graduation. What is the reading?
notes.explanation: Barrel plus thimble plus vernier: 0.425 + 0.008 + 0.0006 = 0.4336 inch, each vernier line being 0.0001.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Vernier Scale”, p. 11-23
notes.evidence: The thimble scale reading is added to it, then the vernier scale reading is added to get the final reading.
notes.choices:
A) 0.439 inch
B) 0.4336 inch
C) 0.4308 inch
D) 0.4256 inch
notes.choicesExplained: A treats the vernier as thousandths (0.425 + 0.008 + 0.006). C misreads the thimble and vernier (0.425 + 0.005 + 0.0008). D leaves out the thimble (0.425 + 0.0006).

notes.front: To be sure of a reading, a mechanic screws the spindle down hard on the work every time. What risk does this create?
notes.back: A: The frame may be sprung permanently, giving inaccurate readings.
notes.explanation: Tightening the spindle too much may permanently spring the frame.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Using a Micrometer”, p. 11-24
notes.evidence: If the spindle is tightened too much, the frame may be sprung permanently and inaccurate readings will result.
notes.choices:
A) The frame may be sprung permanently, giving inaccurate readings
B) The anvil becomes magnetised
C) The vernier scale shifts by 0.001
D) None; firm pressure improves accuracy
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are not effects the handbook describes. D is the mistake itself.

notes.front: You need to check an aircraft brake disc for warp while rotating it. Which instrument fits?
notes.back: A: Dial indicator.
notes.explanation: The handbook names checking for warp in a rotating component such as a brake disc as a common dial indicator use.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Using a Micrometer”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: Another common use for the dial indicator is to check for a warp in a rotating component, such as a brake disc.
notes.choices:
A) Dial indicator
B) Outside micrometer
C) Hermaphrodite caliper
D) Borescope
notes.choicesExplained: B measures a fixed dimension. C is a marking gauge. D is for seeing inside areas.

notes.front: You must measure the inside diameter of a bushing and the depth of a blind hole with one tool. Which suits best?
notes.back: A: A slide caliper with a depth gauge.
notes.explanation: Slide caliper jaws measure inside and outside dimensions, and some calipers contain a depth gauge for blind holes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Slide Calipers”, p. 11-25
notes.evidence: Some slide calipers also contain a depth gauge for measuring the depth of blind holes.
notes.choices:
A) A slide caliper with a depth gauge
B) A steel rule
C) An outside micrometer
D) Dividers
notes.choicesExplained: B is less accurate and has no jaws. C measures outside dimensions. D transfers measurements.

notes.front: A shop torque wrench fell off a bench, and its dial glass is now cracked. What should happen before it is used again?
notes.back: D: Test it, since signs of rough handling were found.
notes.explanation: A cracked dial glass or signs of rough handling mean the wrench must be tested.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Torque Wrench”, p. 11-6
notes.evidence: If a bent pointer, cracked or broken glass (dial type), or signs of rough handling are found, the wrench must be tested.
notes.choices:
A) Use it; the glass is cosmetic
B) Tape the glass and carry on
C) Use it only on noncritical bolts
D) Test it, since signs of rough handling were found
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C use an instrument whose accuracy is now in doubt.

notes.front: You want to measure a resistor still wired in a powered circuit. What should you do before connecting the ohmmeter?
notes.back: B: Remove power and disconnect or isolate the resistor.
notes.explanation: The component must be isolated and power removed; disconnecting the resistor prevents damage to the ohmmeter and false readings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Tracing Opens with the Ohmmeter”, p. 12-82
notes.evidence: When an ohmmeter is used, the circuit component to be tested must be isolated and the power source removed from the circuit.
notes.choices:
A) Switch to the highest range and measure
B) Remove power and disconnect or isolate the resistor
C) Measure twice and average
D) Ground one lead to the airframe
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D leave the meter connected to a live, parallel circuit.

notes.front: Annual and 100-hour inspections have identical scope. Besides who may do them, what is the other difference?
notes.back: A 100-hour limit may be overflown by up to 10 hours to reach a place where the inspection can be done.
notes.explanation: The annual inspection has no such flight-hour allowance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Annual/100-Hour Inspections”, p. 10-5
notes.evidence: The other difference involves authorized overflight of the maximum 100 hours before inspection. An aircraft may be flown up to 10 hours beyond the 100-hour limit if necessary to fly to a destination

notes.front: How do continuous inspection programmes differ from progressive ones?
notes.back: They apply to large or turbine-powered aircraft and are more complicated; both need approval.
notes.explanation: Airlines use them with routine and detailed inspections at increasing levels, the A- to D-checks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Continuous Inspections”, p. 10-12
notes.evidence: Continuous inspection programs are similar to progressive inspection programs, except that they apply to large or turbine-powered aircraft and are therefore more complicated.

notes.front: How does a hard landing inspection differ from an overweight landing inspection?
notes.back: Hard: landings at or below maximum design landing limits. Overweight: landing above maximum design landing weight.
notes.explanation: Stress depends on gross weight and on severity of impact.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Hard or Overweight Landing Inspection”, p. 10-14
notes.evidence: The hard landing inspection is for hard landings at or below the maximum design landing limits. An overweight landing inspection must be performed when an airplane lands at a weight above the maximum design landing weight.

notes.front: How do penetrant and magnetic particle inspection differ in the depth of defects they find?
notes.back: Penetrant finds only defects open to the surface; magnetic particle finds surface and subsurface discontinuities.
notes.explanation: Magnetic particle, though, is limited to ferromagnetic materials.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Advantages & Disadvantages of NDI Methods”, p. 10-19
notes.evidence: Detects surface and subsurface discontinuities • Relatively fast • Surface must be accessible

notes.front: How do circular and longitudinal magnetisation differ?
notes.back: Circular: current through the part, concentric field. Longitudinal: part in a solenoid, field along the long axis.
notes.explanation: Two operations are needed because defects can lie at any angle to the axis.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Effect of Flux Direction”, p. 10-30
notes.evidence: This requires two separate magnetizing operations, referred to as circular magnetization and longitudinal magnetization.

notes.front: How do the continuous and residual magnetic particle procedures differ?
notes.back: Continuous: medium applied while magnetising force is on. Residual: applied after it is removed, using remaining magnetism.
notes.explanation: Continuous is more sensitive but reveals more nonsignificant discontinuities.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnetizing Methods”, p. 10-31
notes.evidence: The residual inspection procedure involves magnetization of the part and application of the indicating medium after the magnetizing force has been removed.

notes.front: How does Magnaglo inspection differ from ordinary magnetic particle inspection?
notes.back: It uses a fluorescent particle solution and is inspected under black light.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the method is similar; the glow lets smaller flaws be seen.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Magnaglo Inspection”, p. 10-32
notes.evidence: Efficiency of inspection is increased by the neon-like glow of defects allowing smaller flaw indications to be seen.

notes.front: How do pulse echo and through-transmission ultrasonic inspection differ?
notes.back: Pulse echo: one transducer reads reflections. Through-transmission: two transducers on opposite surfaces; less sensitive to small defects.
notes.explanation: A disrupted sound path, not a reflection, shows the flaw in through-transmission.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Through-Transmission”, p. 10-24
notes.evidence: A disruption in the sound path indicates a flaw and is displayed on the instrument screen.

notes.front: How do dividers and pencil compasses differ?
notes.back: Dividers have both legs tapered to needle points; pencil compasses have one needle leg and one pencil leg.
notes.explanation: On metal, dividers scribe only arcs or circles that are later cut away; all others are drawn with pencil compasses to avoid scratching the material.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Dividers and Pencil Compasses”, p. 11-19
notes.evidence: Pencil compasses have one leg tapered to a needle point. The other leg has a pencil or pencil lead inserted. Dividers have both legs tapered to needle points.

notes.front: How does a tap differ from a die?
notes.back: A tap cuts internal threads in a hole; a die cuts external threads on round stock.
notes.explanation: Adjustable split dies can be spread to control thread fit; solid dies cannot.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Taps and Dies”, p. 11-14
notes.evidence: Solid dies are not adjustable. Therefore, a variety of thread fits cannot be obtained with this type.
